## Today's question

Duckweed is a small aquatic plant that floats as tiny leaf-like fronds. In our
simulated study, twenty flasks started with equal amounts of duckweed; ten were
randomly given extra nutrients and ten were controls. After seven days the dry
biomass in each flask was weighed. **How much more biomass did the nutrient
flasks produce, and how certain is that difference?**

Today you answer this on your own, from the raw file to a rendered report, using
what you learned in weeks 2–4. The flask is the independent unit: the fronds in
one flask share its water and nutrients. One nutrient flask, F17, was spilled
before weighing, so its biomass is missing. The full design is in
[data/README.md](../data/README.md).

If your teacher chooses the organic-laboratory study instead, skip to
[The organic alternative](#the-organic-alternative) and do that one only.

**Save today:** `duckweed-report.Rmd` and its HTML, `reports/study-decisions.txt`,
`algae-transfer.R` and `reports/algae-transfer.txt`.

## A plan before the code

Before writing code, write five lines in `reports/study-decisions.txt`: the
question, the independent unit, the outcome and its units, what you will do with
the missing F17, and the direction of the comparison (nutrient minus control).
These decisions shape every later step, and writing them first keeps the code
and the text in agreement.

## Is the file what the design says?

Use **Save As** on the root `report.Rmd` to create `duckweed-report.Rmd`, replace
the title and the seedling text, and load the data:

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
```

Use `count(duckweed, treatment)` to find out how many flasks are in each group,
`anyDuplicated(duckweed$flask_id)` to find out whether any flask appears twice,
and `sum(is.na(duckweed$biomass_mg))` to find out how many flasks have no
biomass. Write each result in the report as a sentence, for example "20 flasks,
10 per group, no duplicates; F17 has no biomass because it was spilled."

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer check

20 rows, 10 control and 10 nutrient, `anyDuplicated()` returns 0, and one
missing biomass value (F17). The biomass values run from 19.8 to 46.2 mg.
:::

## How much biomass is in each group?

Use `group_by()` and `summarise()` to find out the number of flasks with a
measurement, the mean and the SD in each group. Then plot every flask:

```r
available <- duckweed |>
  filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))
```

`available` holds the 19 flasks with a measurement, while `duckweed` keeps F17's
row. Make an individual-point plot of `available` with `treatment` on the x-axis
and `biomass_mg` on the y-axis, with the label "Dry biomass after seven days
(mg)", and state in the caption that F17 is missing.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint and answer check

In `summarise()`, use `n_available = sum(!is.na(biomass_mg))`,
`mean_mg = mean(biomass_mg, na.rm = TRUE)` and `sd_mg = sd(biomass_mg, na.rm = TRUE)`.
For the plot, reuse the week 3 point plot with horizontal jitter only.

Control: 10 flasks, mean **32.28 mg**, SD 5.70 mg. Nutrient: 9 flasks, mean
**39.63 mg**, SD 4.79 mg. The groups overlap: nutrient flask F11 (31.7 mg) is
below most controls, and control F08 (19.8 mg) is low but has no recorded error.
:::

## How large is the nutrient effect?

The flasks are independent and were randomly allocated, so the Welch test from
day 17 fits. Use `t.test()` to find out the nutrient-minus-control difference
and its 95% confidence interval:

```r
nutrient <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg)
comparison
```

Nutrient comes first, so the result is nutrient minus control.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer check

Difference **7.35 mg** (39.63 − 32.28), 95% CI **2.27 to 12.44 mg**, p = 0.0072.
The whole interval lies above zero, so the nutrient flasks produced more
biomass on average.
:::

## Writing the result

Write a paragraph with the direction and size of the difference in mg, the
number of flasks in each group, the confidence interval and p-value, and one
limitation, such as the missing F17 or the small size of the study. Use an inline
result, for example <code>&#96;r round(comparison$conf.int[1], 2)&#96;</code>, for at least one
number, so the text updates itself when the data change.

A classmate wrote this draft. Find what is wrong with it before you write yours:

> "There were 20 biomass results. The nutrient plants all grew more, and the
> group SD is the error in the treatment effect. The p-value tells us the
> probability that nutrients work."

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What is wrong

There are 20 flasks but 19 measurements, because F17 is missing. The groups
overlap, so only the **mean** is higher, not every flask. The SD describes how
much single flasks vary; the uncertainty of the difference is the confidence
interval. The p-value is calculated assuming no difference: it says how
surprising the data would be if nutrients had no effect, not how likely it is
that they work.
:::

Save the report, restart R and render. Before you finish, check:

- Can a reader find the question, the flask as the unit, and why there are 19 values?
- Do the plot, the table and the text give the same numbers?
- Does the sign of the difference agree with the order in `t.test()`?
- Does the report run without anything typed in the Console first?

## The organic alternative {#the-organic-alternative}

Do this study **instead of** the duckweed report if your teacher selects it.
Twelve synthesis runs, procedures that make a chemical product, were randomly
assigned a `standard` or a `modified` collection protocol, six each. For each
run, the file gives the maximum possible product mass (`theoretical_mass_g`)
and the dry product actually collected (`isolated_mass_g`). Runs started at
different scales, so grams cannot be compared directly, but the **percentage
yield** can:

```text
yield (%) = 100 × isolated mass (g) / theoretical mass (g)
```

**Question:** which protocol collected a larger percentage of the possible
product? Save the report as `organic-study.Rmd`; if you made `organic-report.Rmd`
on day 15, keep it and use **Save As**.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- organic |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
```

Check Y01 by hand: 0.62 g of 1.00 g possible is 62%. Then use `group_by()` and
`summarise()` to find out the mean yield and SD in each protocol, and plot
every run. Each run is one independent unit; weighing a product three times
would still be one run. Save a summary CSV and the plot in `output/` with names
starting `organic-`. A descriptive comparison is all this study needs: there is
no test today. Write a result paragraph and render.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer check

Six runs per protocol, no missing values. Standard: mean **68.67%**, SD 4.32
percentage points. Modified: mean **77.00%**, SD 3.74. The modified protocol
collected **8.33 percentage points** more on average. That is a difference of
percentage points, not an 8.33% relative increase. Purity was assumed, not
measured, so a higher yield says nothing about how pure the product is.
:::

## A new dataset: algae cultures

Can you apply the same steps to data you have not seen before? In
`data/algae.csv`, 24 algae cultures were grown separately and randomly given a
`reference` or a `supplement` treatment, twelve each, and harvested after seven
days. Culture A19 was spilled before weighing. The outcome is dry biomass in mg.

Write a short script, `algae-transfer.R`, that imports the file and uses the
same functions as above to find out:

1. how many cultures have a measurement in each group;
2. the mean and SD of biomass in each group, and the supplement-minus-reference
   difference;
3. whether every supplement culture produced more than every reference culture
   (make an individual-point plot).

Save the summary and plot in `output/` with names starting `algae-transfer`, and
write a short result paragraph in `reports/algae-transfer.txt`. Restart R and run
the script from the top. Day 24 will turn it into a report that someone else
can reproduce.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer check

24 unique cultures; 12 reference and 11 supplement measurements, with A19 kept as
`NA`. Reference: mean **28.20 mg**, SD 7.26 mg. Supplement: mean **33.92 mg**,
SD 3.37 mg. Supplement minus reference: **+5.72 mg**. Not every supplement
culture is higher: the largest single value, 41.7 mg, is reference culture A11.
Putting 0 for A19 would wrongly lower the supplement mean to 31.09 mg.
:::

**Leave with:** `duckweed-report.Rmd` (or `organic-study.Rmd`) and its HTML,
`reports/study-decisions.txt`, `algae-transfer.R`, and
`reports/algae-transfer.txt`. Note anything that failed.
